newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate passes five-year tax-cut bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate passes five-year tax-cut bill.

text.p: The Senate on Friday joined the House in approving legislation that will give Americans their biggest tax cut in 16 years and pave the way towards enactment of an agreement balancing the federal budget.

The Senate voted 80-18 to approve the five-year $77 billion net tax cut that would implement the tax portion of last month's pact between congressional leaders and the White House to balance the budget over five years.

"We can go home ... during this Independence Day recess with our heads held high," Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican said. "We have done what our constituents sent us here to do," he said.
House and Senate negotiators in coming weeks will try to work out differences in the two bills before a final package can be sent to President Bill Clinton.
The White House reiterated on Friday that both bills were unacceptable to the president in their present form.

Clinton, however, said he was "quite optimistic" the White House and Congress would reach agreement on the details. "We should expect a little of this skirmishing. We're going to offer our thoughts on Monday," Clinton said.

The Senate defeated a proposal from Sen. Edward Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat, to raise the cigarette tax by 23 cents per pack to pay for children's health programmes. That would have been in addition to the 20-cent-per-pack tobacco tax increase already in the Senate bill.
Senate Budget Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, was angered by the administration's support of Kennedy's proposal, saying it violated the budget agreement.
One amendment that was approved would gradually increase the amount of tax deduction self-employed individuals could take for health insurance, eventually reaching 100 percent.
The Senate bill passed with wide bipartisan support, including the vote of Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota.
"This is truly a celebration of a bipartisan effort to provide tax relief to every taxpayer at every stage of life," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, said.

The Senate bill would provide a $500 tax credit for each child under age 17 and require that the credit be deposited in a type of Individual Retirement Account for education for children aged 13 to 16.
Also included were tax relief for college education costs and expanded Individual Retirement Accounts.

Married couples would be allowed to exclude from taxation up to $500,000 of gain made from selling a home. The bill would cut the capital gains tax on profits made on investments such as stocks to 20 percent from the maximum 28 percent rate for individuals.

The bill would raise the threshold where the estate tax is imposed to $1 million in 2006 from $600,000 now, and immediately exclude $1 million from tax when a family-owned business accounted for more than 50 percent of the estate.

Higher taxes and elimination of certain tax breaks would raise $66 billion in revenues over five years. Those included extension of airline ticket taxes and higher passenger fees, a 20-cent-per-pack increase in the cigarette tax, and a gradual reduction in the ethanol subsidy starting in 2001.
